extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (faculty), prospective/serving editors, and department chairs
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for editing conference proceedings and books, dealing with editors, and serving as (or becoming) a mathematics department chair. Covers editorial roles, production requirements, interpersonal norms, and administrative strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require refereeing for conference proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Conference proceedings papers should be refereed; editors must obtain referee reports and decide which papers to publish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Play 'musical chairs' with refereeing (send paper of participant A to participant B). Make clear you want a serious refereeing job but also that you expect to publish most works of most participants. Endeavor to obtain constructive referee's reports that have useful recommendations about both the mathematics and the writing so you can maintain quality while treating contributors fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and enforce page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Set page limits on papers for the proceedings and enforce them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid a collection of 100-page-long semi-unreadable diatribes; instead aim for a book that will be a milestone and accessible to those learning the area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage survey articles as anchors
rubrics_metrics.description: Include survey articles in a proceedings volume to serve as anchors that hold the project together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convince some participants to write survey articles; the editor might consider writing one. Choose authors for these seminal pieces carefully because they underpin the other papers and give the volume substance and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a strong, compelling introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The proceedings volume should have a strong introduction that explains the conference, the subject, the papers, and the participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate the subject and papers to any dedicatee if applicable; the introduction can be three or four or more pages, fulsome and detailed but not bogged down in extraneous tedium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the AMS (or publisher) preparation checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a publisher's checklist (e.g., AMS checklist) as a touchstone for preparing proceedings and many books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checklist items cited include: check the size of the type block; carefully proofread entire manuscript; obtain necessary permissions; ensure figures are rendered in PostScript at proper resolution; acknowledge grant and contract support; include 2000 Mathematics Subject Classification numbers and key words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obtain constructive reports addressing both mathematics and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees' reports should give useful recommendations about the mathematics and about the writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insist on serious refereeing that helps authors improve both technical content and exposition so quality is maintained without alienating contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquisitions Editor: attract and recruit authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acquisitions Editor finds authors for a book series and attracts books to the publisher's program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This editor often visits campuses and meetings to find or persuade potential authors; their purpose is to bring projects into the company's publishing program.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production Editor: oversee manuscript-to-press process
rubrics_metrics.description: The Production Editor oversees developing a book from manuscript to press-ready format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks include copy editing, art editing, page composition, accuracy checking, and coordinating other production procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy Editor: ensure grammar, consistency, and usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The Copy Editor painstakingly checks grammar, syntax, accuracy, and consistency in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good Copy Editor knows style guides (e.g., Chicago Manual of Style) deeply, can distinguish fine usage (e.g., 'comprise' vs 'compose'), and will work with the author to fix rough spots; working well with a Copy Editor improves your book substantially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Editor: produce publication-quality figures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Art Editor is an expert on graphic design and on software for producing art, responsible for turning supplied artwork into publication-quality graphics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They handle hand-drawn sketches, software-generated figures, or borrowed pictures and ensure final figures reflect well on the author and publisher; familiarity with graphics tools (e.g., Illustrator, xfig) is relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design Editor: control cover and page design appropriate to audience
rubrics_metrics.description: A Design Editor handles cover design, page design, layout of page elements, and overall 'feel' appropriate to the intended market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Market expectations differ (e.g., flashy colors for engineering audience vs subdued look for mathematics). For elementary textbooks design is especially important; for advanced monographs the process is lower-key.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developmental Editor: shepherd elementary textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: For elementary books a Developmental Editor oversees reviewing, helps interpret reviews, recommends revisions and augmentations, supervises design, and shepherds the project to completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good developmental editor is a blessing; a bad one can be a nightmare; their role includes overseeing copy and art editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Editorial Assistants to manage logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial Assistants keep track of papers, editors, referees, deadlines, typesetter/printer interactions, and bring problems to the editor's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They do the legwork so the editor can focus on decisions; a good assistant makes the editor far more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial Board: attract authors and provide imprimatur
rubrics_metrics.description: For a book series, consulting editors and an editorial board attract authors, select topics, and review manuscripts; for journals the editorial board is the union of editors with associate editors doing the refereeing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The board lends credibility to a series; for journals, the Managing Editor oversees operations and makes final publication decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deal with editors politely and constructively
rubrics_metrics.description: When interacting with book or journal editors, respond politely, listen to suggestions, and be constructive rather than arrogant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that editorial staff often know the marketplace and language usage limits; disagree courteously if needed. Maintain a good working relationship, keep editors informed of progress and roadblocks, and socialize (e.g., AMS/MAA meetings) to build rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work with copy/production editors on prose and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors can help shore up syntax, style, and organization in mathematical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to their advice; they can significantly improve clarity and usability of your book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt teaching and expectations as a foreign faculty member
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign-born instructors must adjust to differences in student preparation, class pace, and university structures in the U.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming students have same sophistication as in your home country; set appropriate exam difficulty; be patient with elementary questions; learn colloquial language to understand students; be willing to re-think pedagogy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be collegial and a team player as a foreign faculty member
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign faculty should cultivate collegiality, cooperation, and integration with the department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refusing to learn local language or failing to be a team player can lead to career problems; make efforts to fit in administratively and socially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage strengths foreign faculty bring
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign colleagues often enrich teaching and department culture by bringing fresh approaches and cultural perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may be popular teachers for their fresh methods, willingness to adapt, and ability to make learning a shared adventure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in national professional service
rubrics_metrics.description: Belong to professional organizations (AMS, MAA, SIAM) and consider serving on national committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Service is informative, can be fun, keeps you informed, and counts (at least a little) on your CV for tenure/promotion; choose committees (e.g., Editorial Boards Committee, Nominating Committee) that are useful or interesting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand Chair vs Head distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: A Chairman is a leader among equals with modest extra pay; a Head is more autonomous and answerable to the Dean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminology varies by institution; the Head may have more unilateral decision power, while a Chair typically works more by consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dean appoints the Chair; be realistic about selection process
rubrics_metrics.description: Although departments may vote or campaign, the Dean ultimately appoints the Chair/Head and the decision is theirs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes vary (campaigns, ballots, private Dean consultations). Terms vary by institution (e.g., 3–5 years or longer for Heads), and the Dean prefers someone dependable they can work with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical prerequisite: senior rank for Chair
rubrics_metrics.description: It is virtually a prerequisite to be a full Professor to serve as Chair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seniority matters because Chairs must handle promotions and personnel issues; exceptions are rare and context-dependent (small departments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair's primary aim: do the most good / minimize harm
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair's primary goal should be to do the most good for the most people most of the time—'First, do no harm.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize harm when faced with compromises; avoid pandering to special interests even if those interests represent excellent scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair responsibilities: strengthen programs and promote research
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful Chair should strengthen undergraduate programs, attract and improve graduate recruitment, recruit outstanding faculty, promote research, and create a convivial productive atmosphere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ponder long-term goals, implement specific policies to effect plans, and enlist help from others to accomplish these aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chair personal qualities: patience, honesty, ethics, dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: A Chair should be patient, honest, uphold ethical standards, and handle disciplinary matters while preserving colleagues' dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid public beratement; let people keep dignity when correcting behavior; be acquainted with AMS Ethics and Ethics in Employment documents and hold others to professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitate faculty governance: run the department openly
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chair should remember the faculty define the department and should facilitate faculty activities rather than dominate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run the department transparently, provide many committees, deputies, and opportunities for voice so everyone feels involved; frequent informal interactions (teas) help keep communication flowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spread decision-making to share power and blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Deputies, Vice-Chairs, Associate Chairs, and many committees to distribute authority and responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spreading power helps involve more people, dilutes blame, and keeps the operation running; this also helps the Chair remain effective and less isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have initiatives but maintain Dean support
rubrics_metrics.description: A good Chair initiates positive change and starts initiatives, but should retain the Dean's support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have a good Dean, they will back you when faculty resist; avoid being perceived as a rabble-rouser by the Dean, since that can cost you support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for attempts to depose the Chair and manage unrest
rubrics_metrics.description: A Chair may face a groundswell to remove them; such actions will bring a list of complaints and put the Dean in a deciding position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deans dislike 'excessive' unrest and will act to ensure the department runs smoothly; maintain open processes and be mindful of when faculty discontent becomes persistent.
